item.title: Safe by design: preparing a Canadian learning app's AI study companion for chatbot safety duties
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Canadian learning app for young people can prepare its AI study chatbot for proposed online safety duties: crisis escalation, no manipulative design, evidence.
item.content:encoded:
A Canadian learning app gave secondary students and young adults an AI study companion. Students used it for homework, and sometimes for things that had nothing to do with homework. With Canada proposing duties for AI chatbot services, including emergency measures for crisis situations and limits on manipulative engagement, the company wanted its chatbot to be safe by design and able to show it, before any rules took effect.

The situation

A Canadian education company ran a learning app used by secondary school students and young adults. Its most popular feature was an AI study companion: a chatbot that explained concepts, quizzed students and helped plan revision. It had a friendly persona, remembered past sessions and was tied into the app's streaks and reminders. Most conversations were about schoolwork. Some were not: exam stress, trouble at home, and occasionally something more serious. The chatbot answered those with whatever the model produced in the moment.

In June 2026 the Government of Canada introduced Bill C-34, the Safe Social Media Act, which would create duties for social media and AI chatbot services and a Digital Safety Commission to oversee them1. For chatbots, the proposed duty to act responsibly includes mitigating the risk of harmful content, putting emergency measures in place for crisis situations and mitigating harmful chatbot behaviour2. Osler notes the proposals also address manipulative engagement techniques that encourage emotional attachment3. The bill was not yet law, but the company's school and parent customers were already asking the same questions.

Why now. Canada's Budget 2026, released on 5 November, proposed $176.3 million over five years for the new commission, a sign that enforcement would be funded, not just legislated4. Building safety in before the rules settled was cheaper than retrofitting it under a deadline.

What had to be true

  • Crisis handled every time: signals detected on every message, with a fixed, tested response and a route to people.
  • No manipulative design: no feature that kept students engaged against their interests.
  • Age-appropriate by default, with stricter settings for younger users.
  • Tested continuously: safety behaviour checked whenever the model, prompts or features change.
  • Evidence on hand: a written safety plan and records that show it works.
  • Privacy respected: conversation data kept only as far as safety needs, under Canada's privacy laws.

Architecture

All model calls went through a gateway that applied policy before and after the model. A dedicated crisis detector ran on every user message, separate from the general content checks, because the cost of missing a crisis is different from the cost of missing an off-topic question. When it fired, the gateway did not call the study model at all. It returned a fixed response, reviewed by clinicians the company worked with, that acknowledged the student and gave crisis resources, including Canada's 9-8-8 helpline, then offered to continue only if the student wanted to.

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: crisis handling and engagement design

Not missing, not over-blocking. A detector tuned too loosely misses students who need help; tuned too tightly, it interrupts a student revising a history essay about war or a novel about grief. We built evaluation sets from reviewed conversations, written with clinicians and teachers, covering clear crises, ambiguous messages and schoolwork that only looks alarming. Every change to the detector, model or prompts ran against them, and misses were treated as serious defects. See evaluation sets that predict production.

Reviewing conversations without over-collecting. Reviewers needed to see what the student said and what the companion replied, as a trace with prompts and outputs, which OpenTelemetry's generative AI conventions make possible to capture as opt-in content5. Conversation content was captured only for flagged cases and samples for evaluation, stored separately with short retention and access logged, rather than logging everything by default; see LLM observability with OpenTelemetry.

Taking manipulation out. The harder conversation was about engagement. The companion had been tuned to keep sessions going, and some streak reminders used guilt ("your companion misses you"). We reviewed every engagement feature against one question: does this serve the student's learning, or only our retention numbers? Guilt-based messages went, the persona stopped expressing feelings about the student's absence, and late-night nudges were switched off for younger users.

A chatbot for young people should be judged by what it does on its worst conversation, not its average one. Design for that conversation first.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Separate crisis detector before the modelRely on the model's own safety behaviourHolds when the model or prompt changes
Fixed, clinician-reviewed crisis responseLet the model respond with careNo improvising in the highest-risk moment
Evaluation sets including schoolwork that looks alarmingCrisis examples onlyMeasures over-blocking as well as misses
Remove guilt-based engagementKeep and soften wordingRetention is not worth emotional pressure on young users
Capture content only for flagged and sampled casesLog every conversationEnough for safety, less exposure for students
Build before the bill passesWait for final rulesThe core measures make sense under any version

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: put the crisis path outside the model. It meant model upgrades never put the most important behaviour at risk. Differently: involve teachers in building evaluation sets from the start; they knew exactly which schoolwork topics would trip a detector. item.title: Tech news, 7 November 2026: an exploited OpenSSH flaw, browser extensions and Claude Dispatch, Microsoft and Oracle, and child online safety in California and Canada
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: an OpenSSH flaw on Alpine exploited within hours, Claude Dispatch research, Microsoft winds down Oracle capacity, and new child online safety fights.
item.content:encoded:
A password bypass in OpenSSH on musl-based Linux, including Alpine, was reportedly exploited within hours of disclosure, a reminder of how much runs on small container images. Researchers showed how a browser extension could steer a desktop AI agent, Microsoft stepped back from older rented AI capacity, and two governments moved in opposite directions on child online safety.

Today's brief covers stories from 5 to 6 November.

1. An OpenSSH flaw on Alpine Linux is exploited within hours

CVE-2026-123158, nicknamed "sshole", lets attackers log in over SSH without a password to certain accounts on Linux systems built on the musl C library without PAM, most notably Alpine Linux; OpenSSH released a fix in version 10.6p2 on 5 November12. Help Net Security reports exploitation began within hours of disclosure, mainly against accounts with no usable password, such as key-only users1. glibc-based distributions such as Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora are reported as not affected2.

CTO take: Alpine is everywhere in containers, appliances and cloud images, often in places nobody thinks of as "a server". Find every Alpine or other musl-based system that runs sshd, patch and rebuild images, and in the meantime disable password authentication or SSH entirely where it is not needed. Longer term, containers should not run SSH at all, and management access belongs on a separate, tightly controlled path; see hardening a management plane.

2. Researchers show a browser extension steering Claude Desktop through Dispatch

Security researchers reported that a malicious or compromised browser extension with access to claude.ai could use Claude's Dispatch feature to make Claude Desktop run commands on a connected computer, which they demonstrated in testing3. They reported no attacks in the wild; coverage differs on whether and how Anthropic will change the feature34.

CTO take: once a desktop agent can act on a machine, everything that can talk to that agent is part of its attack surface, including browser extensions. Manage extensions with an allowlist on company browsers, keep human approval for agents running commands locally, and avoid automatic approval settings on machines with sensitive access. See agentic infrastructure and prompt injection defence for agents.

3. Microsoft winds down rented AI capacity from Oracle

Microsoft is winding down a 2023 arrangement to rent AI computing from Oracle, reportedly because the capacity ran on older Nvidia chips that no longer met its needs, The Next Web reports, citing Bloomberg5. Oracle said demand for its AI infrastructure remains strong, including for earlier-generation GPUs5.

CTO take: AI hardware ages fast, and a contract for a specific chip generation can become poor value well before it ends. When you reserve capacity, prefer terms tied to performance or allowing upgrades, keep commitments shorter than the hardware's useful life, and keep workloads able to move. See planning around the AI capacity crunch and the multi-region AI capacity case study.

4. Google, Meta and TikTok sue to block California's youth social media law

Google, Meta and TikTok filed separate lawsuits to block a California law, due to take effect on 1 January 2027, that restricts features such as addictive feeds, endless scrolling and autoplay for users under 16, arguing it violates the First Amendment6.

CTO take: whatever the courts decide, the direction of travel is clear: age-aware product behaviour is becoming a legal requirement in more places. Products with younger users should be able to switch features on or off by age and jurisdiction through configuration, not code changes. See New York's youth chatbot law and the US page.

5. Canada funds a new online safety regulator covering AI chatbots

Canada's Budget 2026, released on 5 November, proposes $176.3 million over five years for a Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission7. BetaKit reports the commission would enforce proposed legislation covering social media and AI chatbot services, with powers including binding orders, audits and fines8.

CTO take: AI chatbots are now named directly in online safety regimes, not just social networks. If you offer a chatbot to the public in Canada, start recording how you assess and reduce risks of harmful content, especially for younger users; the same evidence will serve in other markets. See where I work.

What I'd do this week

  • Inventory Alpine and other musl-based systems running sshd, patch to OpenSSH 10.6p2 and rebuild images.
  • Review browser extension policies on machines that run desktop AI agents.
  • Check reserved AI capacity contracts for chip generation and upgrade terms.
  • Make age and jurisdiction a configuration in consumer products.

item.title: Agentic infrastructure: the skills, tools, sandboxes and controls that let AI agents do real work safely
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: The layers a company needs to run AI agents in production: skills, MCP tools, sandboxes, identity, workflows and telemetry, and what to build first.
item.content:encoded:
Most companies started with agents as a chat window and a few API calls. Agents that do real work need more underneath them: packaged know-how they can load when needed, tools with clear permissions, somewhere safe to run code, an identity for every action, and a record of what happened. This is the stack I design for teams moving agents from demos to production, layer by layer, with the standards that now exist for each.

From chat window to infrastructure

An agent is a model in a loop: it reads a goal, decides on a step, calls a tool, looks at the result and repeats. That loop is easy to demo and hard to run at scale. Once agents touch real systems, the same questions come up in every company: how does the agent know how we do things here, what is it allowed to touch, where does its code run, whose authority is it acting on, and how do we find out what it did? Each question maps to a layer of infrastructure, and in 2026 most layers have an emerging standard.

Skills: packaged know-how, loaded when needed

A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file: a short name and description, then instructions, optionally alongside scripts, templates and reference documents1. The agent sees only the names and descriptions up front and reads the full skill when a task calls for it, so a company can give an agent hundreds of procedures without filling its context window1. Anthropic published the format as an open specification, and many agent tools now read the same files2.

For a business, skills are the natural home for "how we do things here": how to write a release note, how to reconcile a payment file, which checks to run before changing a database. They are also where tool automation becomes reliable. If a step is deterministic, put a script in the skill and tell the agent to run it, rather than letting the model regenerate the logic each time. The model handles judgement; code handles the parts that must be the same every time.

Treat skills as code. A skill can contain scripts that run with the agent's permissions, so a skill from the internet deserves the same scrutiny as a dependency. Keep company skills in version control, review changes, publish them through an internal registry and only allow approved sources. See running an enterprise MCP sub-registry for the same pattern applied to tools.

Tools: what the agent can actually do

Tools are how agents act: query a database, open a ticket, send a message, deploy a change. The Model Context Protocol has become the common way to expose them, and its 2026-07-28 specification made the protocol core stateless and added a formal extensions framework, which makes MCP servers easier to run behind ordinary load balancers3. See the MCP stateless migration playbook.

Design tools for agents, not for humans. Fewer, task-shaped tools ("create refund up to a limit") are safer and easier for a model to use than thin wrappers around every API endpoint. Mark which tools only read and which change things, and require approval for the ones that are hard to undo. The MCP server security checklist covers the details.

SkillToolWorkflow
What it isInstructions and scriptsA callable capabilityA fixed sequence of steps
Best forHow to do a task wellActing on a systemSteps that must always happen in order
Who decides the next stepThe agent, guidedThe agentThe code
Main riskMalicious or stale contentToo much permissionRigid when reality differs

Execution: sandboxes and workflows

Agents that write and run code need somewhere disposable to do it. The Kubernetes Agent Sandbox project, under SIG Apps, adds a Sandbox resource for isolated, stateful, single-instance workloads, with support for runtimes such as gVisor and Kata Containers, scale to zero when idle and warm pools to avoid cold starts5. That fills a real gap: an agent's workspace looks nothing like a stateless web service. See scale to zero on Kubernetes for the cost side.

Isolation is necessary but not sufficient, as the CNCF has argued6. A perfectly isolated sandbox holding a broad API key can still do damage through that key. Pair sandboxes with limited outbound network access, short-lived credentials scoped to the task, and monitoring of what leaves the sandbox; see agent sandboxing lessons and prompt injection defence.

Long-running work also needs a workflow layer: durable queues, retries, timeouts and human approval steps that survive restarts. Let the workflow own the order of steps that must always happen, such as "approve before payment", and let the agent work inside each step.

Control: identity, policy and a stop button

Every action an agent takes should answer two questions: which agent did it, and on whose authority. The MCP Enterprise-Managed Authorization extension, now stable, lets organisations grant MCP server access centrally through their identity provider, scoped to users' groups and roles, instead of each user authorising each server4.

On top of identity, define policy per agent: which tools, which data, what spending or volume limits. And keep a stop button: a way to pause one agent, or revoke its credentials, in seconds. See the 4 November tech news on agent kill switches.

Evidence: telemetry, evaluations and cost

OpenTelemetry's generative AI semantic conventions define spans for agent invocations and tool executions alongside model calls, so a single trace can show what the agent was asked, which tools it called and what each cost in time and tokens7. Use them from the start; retrofitting telemetry onto agents in production is painful. Then run evaluations on real tasks whenever a model, skill or tool changes; see evaluating AI agents.

What to build, in order

Agents get more useful as you give them more skills and tools. They get safe enough to keep only when every action has an identity, a limit and a record.

CTO take

The interesting work in agentic AI has moved from the model to the infrastructure around it. Skills turn tacit company knowledge into something an agent can use and a reviewer can read. MCP makes tools portable. Sandboxes and workflows make execution safe and durable. Identity and telemetry make the whole thing governable. None of these needs a large platform team to start: a registry of approved skills and tools, agent identities in your existing identity provider and OpenTelemetry on every call will take most teams a long way. For how far to let agents run unattended, see dark factories and automating work, and for a worked example, the enterprise MCP agent platform case study.

How I can help

I design agent platforms: skills and tool registries, sandboxed execution, identity and policy, and the telemetry that shows what agents actually do. item.title: Clock-ready: Cyber Resilience Act vulnerability handling for a German industrial software maker, as AI-found reports surge
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a German industrial software maker can meet EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting duties as AI-found vulnerability reports surge: triage, SBOMs and signed fixes.
item.content:encoded:
A German company sold machine-monitoring software to manufacturers across Europe: an edge gateway installed in factories and a cloud application. From September 2026 the EU Cyber Resilience Act required it to report actively exploited vulnerabilities on tight deadlines. At the same time, vulnerability reports were arriving faster, many of them written with AI. The company needed a product security process that could separate signal from noise, know which customers were exposed and start the regulatory clock at the right moment.

The situation

A German software company sold machine-monitoring software to manufacturers across Europe. Its product had two parts: an edge gateway installed on factory networks that collected data from machines, and a cloud application where customers viewed dashboards and alerts. Both were built on many open-source components. Security reports came in through a shared email address, were picked up by whichever engineer had time, and were tracked in the general bug tracker. Nobody could quickly say which customers ran which gateway release, or which releases contained a given library.

The product counted as a product with digital elements under the EU Cyber Resilience Act. From 11 September 2026, manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents, once, through ENISA's Single Reporting Platform, which passes them to the relevant national CSIRT and ENISA12. The first step is an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware of active exploitation, followed by a fuller notification and a final report2. An email inbox and goodwill could not meet those deadlines reliably.

Why now. Vulnerability reports were getting more numerous and harder to judge. On 5 November 2026 OpenAI released GPT-6 Cyber, a model for authorised vulnerability research that it rates at its highest cybersecurity risk level3. OpenAI's own security leadership has said AI-generated reports are overwhelming some open-source maintainers4, and projects such as Debian have begun experimenting with AI-assisted triage to cope5. The company was seeing the same pattern at its own scale: more reports, some excellent, many duplicated or unreproducible.

What had to be true

  • One way in: every report, from researchers, customers, suppliers or internal scanners, reaches one queue with an owner.
  • Noise filtered cheaply, without letting a real vulnerability sit unread.
  • Exposure answerable fast: for any component, which releases contain it and which customers run them.
  • A consistent start to the clock: a written rule for when the company is "aware" of active exploitation.
  • Fixes customers can trust: signed releases and advisories that say what to do.
  • Evidence kept: who knew what, when, and what was reported.

Architecture

The core was a security case record, separate from the general bug tracker, with restricted access. Every report became a case with an owner, a status and a timeline. The build pipeline produced a CycloneDX SBOM for every gateway and cloud release, and the licensing system already knew which customer ran which gateway release, so joining the two gave a direct answer to "who is exposed?". When a vulnerable library was present but its vulnerable code was not reachable, the team published a VEX statement saying so, which cut down repeated questions from customers' scanners.

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: AI triage and the start of the clock

Treating reports as untrusted input. Using a language model to read incoming reports helped with volume, but reports are written by strangers, and some could contain instructions aimed at the model. The triage model therefore had no tools, no access to code or customer data, and only produced a structured summary: claimed component, claimed impact, duplicate candidates and missing information. It could not close a case. Anything it marked as low quality still had a person glance at it before closing. See prompt injection defence for agents.

Defining "aware". The 24-hour early warning runs from when the manufacturer becomes aware of active exploitation1. A report that a flaw exists is not the same as evidence that someone is exploiting it. With the company's lawyers, we wrote a short rule: credible evidence of exploitation, such as a customer incident, a national CERT notice, a public exploit used in attacks or an entry in an exploited-vulnerability catalogue, starts the clock, and the on-call lead records the time and the evidence. Borderline cases went to a named second person within working hours, with a bias toward reporting early.

Shipping fixes to factories. Gateways sat on factory networks where customers controlled update timing. Signed releases, verifiable before installation, meant customers' operations teams could accept updates without a call to the vendor6. Advisories listed affected versions, the fixed version and a workaround for sites that could not update immediately.

Regulation sets the deadline; your inventory decides whether you can meet it. If you cannot say who runs which release, no process can report on time.

How it ran

A tabletop exercise, run before any real case, walked through a mock exploited vulnerability from report to final submission. It found gaps that documents had hidden: who held access to the reporting platform at weekends, and which customer contacts were out of date.

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Separate security case recordGeneral bug trackerRestricted access and a clean timeline for reporting
AI sorts, people decideAI closes low-quality reportsA missed real vulnerability costs far more than review time
Triage model with no tools or data accessAgent that inspects codeReports are untrusted input
Written exploitation rule agreed with legalJudgement case by caseThe clock starts consistently and defensibly
SBOM joined to customer inventorySBOM files on their ownAnswers "who is exposed?", not just "what is inside?"
Signed releases with advisoriesRelease notes onlyFactory teams can verify and act without a call

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: build the release-to-customer map before anything else. It turned every later question from an investigation into a lookup. Differently: run the tabletop exercise in the first weeks, not after the process was written; it would have shaped the runbook rather than corrected it. Related: defender-first AI models and vulnerability management, AI model supply chain security, the 6 November tech news and the Europe page.

item.title: Tech news, 6 November 2026: OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber, an AI stock selloff, Google in Wyoming, Micron pauses in Taiwan and an exploited Apple flaw
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: OpenAI's gated GPT-6 Cyber, a 5.5% Nasdaq drop on AI fears, Google's $17B Wyoming data centre, Micron's Taiwan pause and an exploited Apple flaw.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI released a cyber model that it rates at its highest risk tier and gates behind an application process. The same day, AI and chip stocks fell sharply as investors weighed the political backlash against data centres, Google answered that backlash with a $17 billion project that pays its own power bill, and a labour dispute paused a memory plant in Taiwan.

Today's brief covers stories from 4 to 5 November.

1. OpenAI releases GPT-6 Cyber to approved security teams

OpenAI released GPT-6 Cyber on 5 November, a version of its GPT-6 Astra model built for authorised vulnerability research, and rated it Critical, the top cybersecurity level in its Preparedness Framework1. Access is limited to approved security teams through an application process, and OpenAI says a Firefox research campaign produced evidence for 81 new vulnerabilities that Mozilla classified as high severity12. Most performance figures so far come from OpenAI's own testing.

CTO take: models that find and confirm bugs at this level shorten the time between a flaw existing and someone exploiting it, whoever gets access first. The defensive response is the same as for earlier cyber models: faster patching, a current inventory of what you run, and capacity to handle more vulnerability reports at once. Security teams that qualify should apply and point the model at their own code. See defender-first AI models and vulnerability management.

2. AI and chip stocks lead a sharp market fall

The Nasdaq Composite fell about 5.5% on 5 November and the S&P 500 about 4.4%, with Xinhua linking the chip selloff to concerns that the midterm results could bring tighter restrictions on data centre construction3. Axios reported that the fall put the Nasdaq into correction territory4.

CTO take: one bad trading day does not change your roadmap, but it is a reminder that much AI pricing and capacity rests on investor confidence. If your plans assume AI costs keep falling and capacity keeps growing, test them against a slower path. Avoid long commitments to a single small provider, and keep the ability to move workloads; see model routing and planning around the AI capacity crunch.

3. Google plans a $17 billion data centre in Wyoming

Google announced a $17 billion data centre in Laramie County, its first in Wyoming, and said it will cover the full cost of the electricity the site uses5. WyoFile reports the project is to be partly powered by a planned fuel cell development with carbon capture, and that the site will use air cooling to protect local water supplies6.

CTO take: after this week's ballot results, paying for your own power and avoiding water use are becoming the price of local consent. Expect new capacity to arrive slowly and in places with spare energy. If you choose cloud regions for AI work, ask your providers where their new capacity is and when it lands; see the multi-region AI capacity case study and the US page.

4. Micron pauses a Taiwan memory plant after a union dispute

Bloomberg reported on 5 November that Micron has largely paused work on a roughly $4.5 billion plant in Taiwan after a dispute with its union over pay7. TheStreet reports the union is seeking a larger share of profits, the plant was meant to make memory for AI servers, and Micron says existing Taiwan operations are unaffected8.

CTO take: high-bandwidth memory is already one of the tightest parts of the AI supply chain, and this adds risk to future supply rather than today's. For most teams it means AI inference prices may stay high for longer, which makes efficiency work worth doing now: smaller models where they are good enough, caching and batching. See the AI memory squeeze and inference architecture and prompt caching.

5. An old Apple flaw is being exploited

CISA added CVE-2024-27834, a flaw affecting several Apple products that was patched in 2024, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 4 November, giving US federal agencies until 18 November to fix it9. The Hacker News reports it is being used to deliver information-stealing malware9.

CTO take: a two-year-old bug being exploited means attackers are counting on devices that were never updated. Check your device management reports for Apple devices on old operating system versions, including ones that can no longer be updated, and decide whether they should still reach company systems.

item.title: Dark factories: what lights-out automation means for factories, software teams and back offices
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Robots run more of the factory floor and AI agents ship code nobody reads. A CTO's view on dark factories in manufacturing, software and back offices.
item.content:encoded:
A dark factory runs without people on the floor, so it needs no lights. The idea is decades old in manufacturing, is spreading fast with the latest wave of industrial robots, and has now been borrowed by software teams whose AI agents write, test and ship code that no human reads. The same question sits behind all three: what has to be true before you can safely take people out of the loop?

An old idea, newly practical

"Lights out" manufacturing is not new. The idea of factories that run unattended has been around for decades, and the term "dark factory" comes from plants that can operate with the lights off because no one needs to see4. What is new is how fast the enabling technology is spreading. The International Federation of Robotics reported in September 2026 that China installed about 354,000 industrial robots in 2025, around 59% of new installations worldwide12.

Even so, fully dark plants remain rare. In a September 2026 report on car manufacturing, experts said they knew of no fully lights-out mass vehicle plant, though some plants have sections where people are hardly seen3. The reality is a spectrum: more of each line runs unattended, while people handle changeovers, maintenance, exceptions and quality decisions.

The same idea, applied to software

In 2026 the term crossed into software. A "dark software factory" is a pipeline where AI agents plan, write, test and ship code with little or no human reading of it. The most discussed example is a security company's small team that described a factory where humans write specifications and watch scores while agents do the rest, a model the Stanford CodeX blog questioned on the grounds of who can trust agent-validated testing7.

The more careful voices draw a lesson from manufacturing. OpenHands argues that the history matters more than the metaphor, and that the approach works best for well-defined work where correctness can be checked automatically5. Addy Osmani describes a spectrum between "light" and "dark" factories, rather than a switch6. That matches the factory floor: most of the value comes long before the last person leaves.

And to back offices

The same pattern is arriving in knowledge work: claims processing, reconciliation, document review, customer service. AI agents read inputs, apply rules and draft outputs, and people review exceptions. The site's case studies show where this works and where it should stop, from repairs triage at a housing association to maintenance planning at an industrial operator. In both, the agents do the reading and drafting, and people keep the decisions that affect customers or physical assets.

What has to be true before you turn the lights off

Whether the line makes phones, software or insurance decisions, the preconditions look the same.

1. You can say precisely what "good" is. A machine can only hit a target it can measure. In software, that means executable specifications and tests that the agents cannot see or edit, so they cannot game them. In back offices, it means written rules and examples of correct outcomes.

2. You can check every output automatically. If quality depends on a person looking, the line is not dark; it has a hidden bottleneck. Invest in verification before generation. See evaluating AI agents.

3. Failures are contained and cheap to undo. Factories isolate a faulty station and replace a part without stopping the line. Software platforms do the same: detect the failed unit, replace it and keep everything else running, as the Kubernetes community describes for large distributed jobs8.

4. Someone can stop the line. Every serious factory has a stop button and someone accountable for pressing it. For agents, that means identity per agent, limits on what each can do, and a way to stop one instantly; see the 4 November tech news on agent kill switches and agent sandboxing.

5. People still understand the system. A plant whose engineers no longer understand its machines cannot improve it or recover from novel failures. A codebase nobody reads builds the same "comprehension debt". Keep people reading the parts that matter most, and design for explainability.

Dark factories are not built by removing people. They are built by making quality measurable, failure recoverable and control explicit, and then removing people from the parts where those three are true.

A sensible path

What it means for teams and hiring

In factories and software alike, the work shifts rather than disappears. Fewer people do the repetitive middle; more of the value sits in specifying what good looks like, building the checks, designing for recovery and handling the exceptions machines cannot. Those roles need deeper understanding of the system, not less. Teams that cut the people who understand the system to fund automation tend to find out why they needed them during the first serious incident. See Team Topologies for AI teams and AI coding policy for engineering teams.

CTO take

The dark factory is a useful destination to think about and a poor target to chase. The organisations getting real value, in manufacturing, software and back offices, are those that invest first in measurable quality, automatic checks, contained failure and clear control, and then automate as far as the evidence allows. That is a playbook any company can start on this quarter, whatever its sector or region. If you are deciding how far to automate, start with a fractional CTO's first 90 days or where I work.

I help teams decide where automation and AI agents can safely run unattended, and build the specifications, checks and controls that make it possible. I am based in India, the United States and the UAE, working globally. See AI architecture or analyse your challenge and bring the result to a call.

item.title: One opt-out for AI training: what the shared robots.txt token changes, and what it does not
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic back one robots.txt opt-out for AI training. A CTO's take on rollout gaps, grounding trade-offs and how to verify crawlers comply.
item.content:encoded:
On 30 October, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic said they will honour a single robots.txt signal for opting out of AI training. For anyone who publishes content, that is simpler than maintaining a list of crawler names. But rollout is uneven, the companies treat AI answers differently from training, and the signal is voluntary. Here is how to decide whether to use it, and how to check it works.

What was agreed

OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic said on 30 October 2026 that they will honour one shared robots.txt token for opting out of AI training, so a single rule can cover all four companies' crawlers; the token is described in an IETF Internet-Draft14. It builds on the IETF's wider work on a shared vocabulary for AI usage preferences5.

The details matter more than the headline. Reporting says Anthropic has begun honouring the token, Microsoft is targeting early 2027 and separates training from grounding with a different tag, Google plans to treat the opt-out like its existing Google-Extended control, which also covers grounding for Gemini answers, and OpenAI has said it aims to implement it in the coming months13. Sources differ on some timings. The signal is voluntary and does not remove content already collected or models already trained2.

Training, grounding and search are three different decisions

The most important practical point is that "AI use" is not one thing. Training puts your content into a model. Grounding fetches your content at answer time and may cite and link you. Search indexing sends people to your site. Opting out of one may or may not affect the others, depending on the company.

For most businesses, the right answer differs by content type. Marketing pages and documentation usually benefit from being cited in AI answers. Paid research, proprietary datasets and member content usually should not train anyone's model for free. That is the same tiering logic as in what Reddit's logged-in move means for content.

A practical rollout

Keep the old rules for now. Until every company has implemented the shared token, keep existing company-specific crawler rules in place; reporting says those continue to work2.

Do not rely on signals for valuable content. Voluntary signals are honoured by companies that choose to honour them. Content that is your competitive asset needs technical controls at your edge, as described in the front-end controls and gateway patterns elsewhere on this site.

Verify, do not assume. Log requests by user agent and path at your edge or in your traces, and check that crawlers stop fetching opted-out sections after the relevant rollout dates. Enriching traces with request headers makes this a simple filter rather than a log-parsing project6.

A robots.txt line is a request, not a lock. Use it to state your preferences clearly, and use your own infrastructure for anything you cannot afford to lose.

Who should act

  • Publishers, marketplaces and data businesses: decide per content tier now, so the token goes in with a clear policy behind it.
  • B2B SaaS and documentation-heavy companies: think twice before opting out of grounding; being cited in AI answers is increasingly how buyers find you. See structured data for AI search.
  • Regulated organisations in the EU, UK and elsewhere: record your choices; they may matter for copyright and AI transparency discussions. See the Europe page.

CTO take

A single opt-out signal backed by four major AI companies is genuinely useful: it lowers the cost of saying no to training. But it arrives in stages, it does not cover the same things at each company, and it remains voluntary. Treat it as one part of a content access policy that separates training, grounding and search, enforces what matters at your edge, and verifies behaviour with your own data. Read alongside the Reddit analysis and where I work.

item.title: Capacity you can move: multi-region AI serving for a US SaaS company when data centres stall
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a US B2B SaaS company can keep AI features fast and affordable when GPU capacity is tight and local opposition slows new data centres: portable, multi-region serving.
item.content:encoded:
A US B2B software company had built AI features that customers now relied on daily. Its model serving sat in one cloud region with one provider, on capacity that was hard to expand. With demand for AI compute outrunning supply and voters pushing back on new data centres, the company needed AI capacity it could move, without rebuilding the product each time.

The situation

A US software company sold a workflow platform to mid-sized businesses. Over two years it added AI features: summarising records, drafting replies, extracting data from documents and an assistant inside the product. Customers adopted them quickly. The company served open-weight models on GPUs in one cloud region, with a managed model API for a few tasks. As usage grew, adding GPU capacity in that region became slow and uncertain, and latency spiked whenever demand peaked.

Why now. Demand for AI compute was running ahead of supply: Fortune reported Microsoft's CFO saying demand for its cloud still exceeded supply3. New capacity was arriving on long timelines and through complex financing, such as Google's credit backstop for Anthropic's Kentucky data centre lease4. And in the 3 November 2026 midterms, voters sided against data centres in 40 of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, according to CNBC's analysis1, a sign of growing opposition to new AI infrastructure2. The board's question was simple: what happens to our AI features if we cannot get more capacity where we are?

What had to be true

  • No single point of capacity: AI features served from more than one region and provider.
  • Moving traffic is configuration, not a code change or a rebuild.
  • Customer data rules respected: some customers required US-only processing; some required specific providers.
  • Costs visible per feature and per customer, so capacity decisions follow value.
  • Quality held when traffic moves between models or providers.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: moving traffic without changing behaviour

Routing is easy to draw and hard to trust. A summary from one model in one region should not read differently from a summary produced somewhere else. The team built a small evaluation set for each AI feature from real, consented examples, and ran it against every model and provider combination the gateway was allowed to use. A route was only enabled for a feature when it passed that feature's evaluation; see evaluation sets that predict production.

The second difficulty was operations. Running identical clusters in two regions doubles the surface area unless they are managed as one. All clusters were built from the same infrastructure code, ran the same serving stack, and were operated from a single multi-cluster view, so engineers could see and act on every region from one place5.

Customer data rules shaped routing as much as capacity did. Some contracts required US-only processing or excluded certain providers. Those rules lived in a per-customer policy the gateway checked on every request, so overflow never sent a restricted customer's data somewhere it should not go. See Kubernetes inference gateway and model routing.

Capacity you cannot move is a dependency you cannot manage. Make moving cheap: same code, same clusters, same evaluations, different place.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Primary plus secondary regionActive-active everywhereResilience without doubling cost
Managed APIs as overflowSelf-host all capacityAbsorbs peaks without buying idle GPUs
Routes enabled per feature after evaluationRoute anywhere with capacityQuality stays consistent when traffic moves
Per-customer data policy in the gatewayRules in each featureOne place to enforce contracts
Cost per feature and customerTotal AI spend onlyCapacity follows value

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with per-request telemetry. It showed that a few features drove most of the cost, which changed the whole capacity plan. Differently: write customer data rules into the gateway before adding the second region; retrofitting them slowed the rollout. Related: planning around the AI capacity crunch, AI cost allocation, the 5 November tech news and the US page.

item.title: Tech news, 5 November 2026: voters push back on data centres, Google backstops Anthropic's lease, an exploited WordPress core flaw and Meta buys Conductor
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: US voters reject data centres at the ballot box, Google backstops Anthropic's $19B lease, a WordPress core flaw is exploited and Meta buys Conductor.
item.content:encoded:
The US midterms delivered an unexpected verdict on AI infrastructure: local voters rejected data centre projects almost everywhere they were asked. Meanwhile the financing behind that infrastructure keeps getting more creative, a flaw in WordPress core's update process is being exploited, and the race to own AI coding tools produced another acquisition.

Today's brief covers stories from 3 to 4 November.

1. US voters reject data centres almost everywhere they were asked

Voters sided against data centres in 40 of 41 data centre-related local ballot measures in 10 states in the 3 November midterms, according to CNBC's analysis based on Ballotpedia data; results were preliminary in some places1. Scientific American reports the results show widespread opposition to AI data centres, with Ohio accounting for many of the measures2.

CTO take: local consent is becoming a real constraint on AI capacity, alongside power and chips. Expect slower new builds in some US regions and more competition for existing capacity. If you depend on reserved GPU capacity in specific US regions, confirm your provider's build plans and keep alternatives in other regions; see planning around the AI capacity crunch and the US page.

2. Google backstops Anthropic's $19 billion data centre lease

TeraWulf disclosed on 4 November that Google will provide credit support for project financing tied to about $19 billion of Anthropic lease commitments at its Kentucky campus, a backstop that falls away if Anthropic achieves and keeps investment grade credit ratings3. TeraWulf also signed a construction agreement with Fluor for the project3.

CTO take: the financing chains behind AI capacity are getting longer, linking model providers, cloud companies, data centre developers and lenders. For buyers, this mostly means capacity arrives on long timelines and is concentrated among a few providers. Keep your stack able to move between providers; see model routing.

3. A WordPress core flaw is being exploited

CISA added a WordPress core vulnerability, CVE-2026-119977, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 3 November4. BleepingComputer reports it is a race condition in WordPress core's update process that attackers have begun exploiting after the patch was released5.

CTO take: WordPress runs a huge share of marketing sites, and many are owned by marketing teams rather than engineering. Find every WordPress site your organisation runs, including agency-hosted ones, confirm they are on the patched release and check for unexpected admin accounts or files. See securing a legacy PHP estate.

4. Meta buys AI coding startup Conductor

Meta has acquired Conductor, a startup whose software lets engineers run several AI coding agents in parallel, Axios reported on 4 November; terms were not disclosed6. Axios also reported that OpenAI said the same day it was acquiring developer tools startup Pierre Computer6.

CTO take: the big labs are buying their way into developers' daily tools. If your teams rely on a small vendor's coding tool, have a plan for it being shut down or changed after an acquisition, as Conductor's cloud service reportedly will be. Keep your coding-agent policy and controls independent of any one tool; see AI coding policy for engineering teams.

What I'd do this week

  • Patch every WordPress site, including ones run by agencies, and check for signs of compromise.
  • Ask your cloud and AI providers about capacity plans in the US regions you depend on.
  • List the small vendors in your AI coding toolchain and what you would do if one disappeared.

item.title: A fractional CTO's first 90 days: listen, map, measure, then change the few things that matter
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: What a fractional CTO should do in the first 90 days: listen, map the system, measure delivery, fix the riskiest gaps, and leave decisions and a plan the team owns.
item.content:encoded:
A fractional CTO has fewer hours than a full-time one and the same expectations. The first 90 days decide whether the engagement creates lasting change or a slide deck. This is the playbook I use: what to look at, what to measure, what to change first, and what to leave behind so the team can carry on without me.

Why the first 90 days matter more for a fractional CTO

A full-time CTO can take six months to find their feet. A fractional CTO typically works a few days a month, often alongside a founder, a head of engineering or a small team. That changes the job. There is no room for long discovery, and no point in decisions that only live in the CTO's head, because the CTO is not there most of the week. The first 90 days have to produce three things: an honest picture of where the technology stands, a small number of changes that reduce real risk, and a way of working the team can run without you. If you are still deciding whether you need one, start with when do you need a fractional CTO.

Days 1 to 30: listen and map

Listen first. Talk to the founders, every engineer, product, support and a few customers if possible. Ask the same questions each time: what slows you down, what breaks, what worries you, and what you would change first. Patterns appear quickly, and the team learns you are there to help rather than to judge.

Map the system. Draw what actually runs: services, data stores, third parties, how code reaches production and who can change what. Mark the risks: single points of failure, unpatched edges, secrets in the wrong places, data with no owner. A one-page map beats a perfect one.

Get basic visibility. If there is little monitoring, start small. The OpenTelemetry community's account of how Skyscanner runs its collectors makes the same point: start with a simple setup and evolve it gradually5. A gateway collector for application telemetry and an agent for infrastructure metrics is often enough to begin with; see OpenTelemetry collector patterns.

Take a baseline. Measure delivery with the four DORA measures, which track how often you deploy, how long changes take to reach production, how often changes fail and how quickly you recover1. Add one or two reliability measures tied to what customers feel. Do not set targets yet; just record where you are. See DORA metrics with AI-assisted engineering.

Days 31 to 60: fix and decide

Close the riskiest gaps. Pick the few risks that could hurt the business most this year, usually security exposure, a fragile deployment process or missing backups, and fix them. Resist the urge to start a rewrite. Small, visible fixes build trust and buy room for bigger changes later.

Write decisions down. Every significant decision gets a short architecture decision record: the context, the decision and its consequences, in the format Michael Nygard described3. For a fractional CTO this is not paperwork; it is how decisions survive the days you are not there. See architecture decision records for fractional CTOs.

Agree reliability expectations. Decide with the founders how much unreliability is acceptable and what happens when it is exceeded. Google's SRE guidance frames this as an error budget: a shared, explicit amount of risk that balances shipping features against stability2. See SLOs and error budgets for small teams.

Shape the team. Look at how work flows between people. Team Topologies offers a useful vocabulary: stream-aligned teams that own a flow of change end to end, supported by platform and enabling teams, with clear interaction modes between them4. Small companies rarely need the full model, but the question of who owns what end to end matters at any size; see Team Topologies for AI teams.

A fractional CTO's best output is not code or slides. It is decisions the team understands, written down, and a team that can keep making good ones.

Days 61 to 90: plan and hand over

Write a short roadmap. One page: the next two or three quarters, the few big bets, what you will not do and why, and how progress will be measured against the baseline. Build it with the team, so it is theirs.

Set an operating rhythm. Agree what happens without you: weekly delivery review, monthly look at the measures, a regular architecture review where new decision records are discussed. Then agree what happens when you are there: the decisions and reviews that need your time.

Be explicit about ownership. List the areas the team owns fully, the ones you co-own, and the ones that still need you. The goal is for the last list to shrink every quarter.

Who does what

Common mistakes

  • Starting with a rewrite. It consumes the engagement and rarely finishes. Fix the riskiest gaps first.
  • Keeping decisions in your head. If it is not written down, it will be reopened the week you are away.
  • Measuring everything. Four delivery measures and one or two reliability ones are enough to steer by.
  • Becoming the bottleneck. If every decision waits for your next visit, you have made the company slower.
  • Ignoring the business. Technology priorities that do not connect to revenue, risk or customers will not survive the next budget conversation.

How I work

This is the shape of most of my engagements, whether the company is a start-up preparing for due diligence, a scale-up whose systems are straining, or a regulated business adopting AI. item.title: Same assistant, different model: launching an AI shopping assistant in China for a foreign consumer brand
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a foreign consumer brand can launch an AI shopping assistant in China: a locally filed model, in-country data, PIPL transfer rules and one shared codebase.
item.content:encoded:
A European consumer brand had an AI shopping assistant that answered product questions and built routines for customers in Europe and the US. China was its fastest-growing market, and the global assistant could not simply be switched on there. The task was to launch a Chinese edition that met local rules, ran on a locally permitted model and kept customer data in China, without forking the product.

The situation

A European skincare and personal care brand sold online and through partners in Europe, the US and China. Its AI shopping assistant answered questions about ingredients and products, built routines from a short questionnaire and handed off to customer service when needed. It ran on a global model provider, with logs and customer profiles in the brand's European cloud. China had its own app, mini-programme and marketplace stores, but no assistant.

Why now. On 31 October 2026, Apple and Alibaba said Alibaba's Qwen will power the China edition of Apple Intelligence, a clear signal that even global platforms ship a different model in China to meet local rules1. China's Interim Measures for generative AI services require qualifying public-facing services to go through filing with the Cyberspace Administration of China2, which publishes lists of filed services in batches3. And the Personal Information Protection Law governs any transfer of Chinese customers' data abroad, with certification measures in effect from 1 January 2026 alongside the standard contract and security assessment routes4. The brand's leadership wanted a Chinese edition for the next sales season, built the right way.

What had to be true

  • A locally permitted model for Chinese users, with the application registered where required.
  • Personal data stays in China: prompts, answers, profiles and logs.
  • One product, not two: shared code and features, with market-specific configuration.
  • Chinese-language quality proven on a local evaluation set before launch.
  • Documentation that follows the design: filing, impact assessment and transfer analysis drawn from the architecture.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: one product, two data worlds

The tempting path was a separate Chinese build: copy the code, swap the model, deploy in China. That would have doubled every future feature and fix. Instead the team moved the product to a task-level AI interface. The application asks for "answer a product question" or "build a routine", and a router decides which model serves it, based on the user's market. Prompts and safety rules became configuration per market, so Chinese prompts could reflect local language, product names and expectations without forking code. See designing AI products with a model per market.

Data was the second half. Product catalogue data is not personal, so it is synced into China. Customer profiles, conversations and logs are created and stored in China and never leave. Telemetry was the easiest thing to get wrong: the global observability stack would have pulled Chinese traces out of the country by default. The team ran a separate telemetry pipeline inside the China environment, using a shared collector with separate pipelines per channel to keep operations simple5, and only aggregated, non-personal metrics are reported to the global dashboard.

Keeping personal data in China also simplified the legal work. With nothing personal designed to leave the country, the assistant did not rely on any of PIPL's transfer mechanisms, a position counsel reviewed, and the impact assessment could describe a clean boundary rather than a set of exceptions4.

Design the boundary first and the paperwork follows. Bolt on compliance after launch and the paperwork becomes the design.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Task-level interface and routerFork the product for ChinaOne codebase, features ship to both
Locally filed model via a Chinese providerUse the global model in ChinaFits the filing regime and local expectations
Personal data stays in ChinaCentral profiles with transfer paperworkSimpler legal position and lower risk
Separate in-country telemetryGlobal observability stackTraces carry personal data; they stay local
Chinese evaluation set before launchTranslate the English testsQuality depends on local language and products

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: refactor to a task-level interface before building the China region. It turned a risky fork into configuration. Differently: build the Chinese evaluation set with the China customer service team from day one; their real questions were the best test material. Related: model routing, evaluation sets that predict production, consent-aware data in India and where I work.

item.title: Tech news, 4 November 2026: a kill switch for AI agents, AMD's data centre surge, BTCPay hot wallet thefts and Android's zero-click fixes
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: CrowdStrike launches a kill switch for rogue AI agents, AMD's data centre revenue nearly doubles, BTCPay hot wallets drained and Android's zero-click fixes.
item.content:encoded:
Security vendors are now selling controls built specifically for AI agents, starting with a way to stop one. AMD's results show how much of the chip market AI data centres have become. And two patching stories, one for self-hosted payment servers and one for every Android phone, round out the day.

Today's brief covers stories from 1 to 3 November that earlier briefs did not include.

1. CrowdStrike launches a kill switch for rogue AI agents

CrowdStrike announced an AI Kill Switch on 3 November that lets administrators stop a misbehaving agent, block it from restarting on targeted hosts and cut its network access; the first version works through connected AI gateways by cutting the agent's access to its models, with broader containment across its platform still to come1. CNBC reports a person still decides when to cut an agent off and when to restore it, and that CrowdStrike also agreed to buy two AI security start-ups2.

CTO take: this confirms where agent control belongs: at a gateway between agents and models, with identity per agent and a clear way to stop one. Whether or not you buy a product for it, you need those three things before agents run in production. See why an AI gateway matters and when agents become the user.

2. AMD's data centre revenue nearly doubles

AMD reported record third-quarter revenue of about $13.4 billion on 3 November, with data centre revenue up 97% year over year to a record $8.5 billion, and guided to about $17 billion for the fourth quarter3.

CTO take: a credible second source of AI accelerators is good news for buyers' negotiating position and capacity planning. Keep your serving stack portable across hardware, for example with vLLM and Kubernetes device abstractions, so you can benchmark and switch; see the AI memory squeeze and DRA for GPU scheduling.

3. Attackers drain hot wallets on outdated BTCPay Servers

Attackers have been draining Bitcoin and Litecoin hot wallets on BTCPay Server installations running version 2.4.1 or earlier; a fix shipped in 2.4.2, and BTCPay told operators running hot wallets to shut down affected servers45. The exact vulnerability behind the latest thefts had not been published at the time of writing5.

CTO take: self-hosted payment software is only as safe as its patch level. If you run it, update, keep only operational funds in hot wallets, rotate credentials and move funds to new wallets if in doubt. The same money-path principles apply as in the Binance lessons.

4. Android's November update fixes zero-click remote code execution

Google's November 2026 Android security bulletin includes critical remote code execution flaws that need no user interaction, affecting Android 14 to 17, along with a denial-of-service bug dubbed "SMS of Death" that can drop calls; reports say the bulletin does not list any issue as exploited6.

CTO take: make sure company-managed devices pick up the November patch level quickly, and set a minimum patch level for apps that handle money or health data. For bring-your-own-device fleets, enforce the minimum through your device management policy.

What I'd do this week

  • Check that every AI agent in production has its own identity, goes through a gateway and can be stopped.
  • Update BTCPay Server if you run it, and reduce hot wallet balances.
  • Push the November Android patch level to managed devices.
  • Ask accelerator vendors for quotes on more than one platform before your next hardware order.

item.title: One week, three signals: HTI-5 is final, a Senate draft rethinks health AI oversight, and WHO Europe sets an AI roadmap
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: In one week the US finalised HTI-5, a Senate draft proposed new AI oversight and payment, and WHO Europe adopted an AI roadmap. What health tech teams should build now.
item.content:encoded:
Between 28 and 29 October, the US finalised a slimmer health IT certification rule that drops its AI model card requirements, the chair of the Senate health committee published a draft bill on AI oversight and payment, and governments across Europe and Central Asia adopted a roadmap for AI in health. Read together, they point to the same thing: less prescriptive federal paperwork in the US, more responsibility on buyers and builders, and a growing expectation of evidence that a model works where it is used.

What happened

HTI-5 is final, and narrower than proposed. The US health IT certification rule was finalised in late October. Legal analyses report it removes 14 of 60 certification criteria rather than the 34 proposed, keeps the privacy and security criteria the proposal would have dropped, defers proposed information blocking changes, and removes the AI "model card" requirements for predictive decision support interventions12. We covered the proposal in From HTI-1 to HTI-5; the final rule confirms the direction on AI transparency while retreating on much else.

A Senate draft rethinks oversight and payment. On 29 October, Senate HELP Committee chair Bill Cassidy released a discussion draft of the PATIENT AI Act. It would clarify whether an AI tool falls under FDA or ONC oversight, let FDA accept premarket software changes, have HHS certify third parties to review lower-risk software, and create a payment pathway for AI-enabled care; comments are due by 1 December34. It is a draft, not law.

WHO Europe sets a direction. The same day, governments across Europe and Central Asia adopted a roadmap for AI in health care, emphasising foundations such as data quality, interoperability, secure access and cybersecurity5.

What it means for builders

In the US, certification will ask less of AI vendors about transparency. That does not mean buyers will. Health systems still have to decide whether a model is safe and useful for their patients, and with less standard documentation, they will ask vendors directly and test more themselves. If the PATIENT AI Act's ideas progress, payment for AI-enabled care would come with expectations of evidence. In Europe, the roadmap points the same way through data quality and interoperability. Different routes, one destination: show the model works, here, on these patients.

Build the evidence anyway

Keep your model facts. Maintain the information the model card requirement covered, such as intended use, training data, known limitations and performance, versioned with every release. It costs little if built into the release process, and buyers will keep asking for it.

Make validation portable. A model that performed well where it was built may not perform well elsewhere. The OHDSI community frames this as evidence attributes: results should be repeatable, reproducible, replicable, generalisable to different data and robust to different analyses6. Mapping site data to a common model such as OMOP lets you run the same validation at each customer; see clinical prediction models on OMOP.

Plan for software change. If FDA gains clearer authority to accept planned software changes, teams with a disciplined change process will move faster. See predetermined change control plans.

Keep FHIR at the centre. The FHIR API criteria stay, and the direction of travel in both the US and Europe is towards standard, secure data access; see TEFCA in 2026.

Regulation sets the minimum. A health system's procurement team sets the bar. Build your evidence for the bar.

Next 90 days

CTO take

The US is stepping back from prescribing AI transparency through certification while exploring how to pay for AI that works, and Europe is investing in the data foundations that make evidence possible. For health tech teams, that adds up to one strategy: own your evidence. Teams that can show, per customer, what their model is, how it performs on that customer's patients and how it is monitored will sell faster under any of these regimes. See healthcare data architecture, the US page and the Europe page.

item.title: Agents that advise, engineers who decide: AI for maintenance planning at a Saudi industrial operator
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Saudi industrial operator can use AI agents to plan maintenance from equipment data, hosted in-Kingdom, with an asset graph, read-only tools and engineer sign-off.
item.content:encoded:
A Saudi industrial operator had decades of equipment history, a work-order system, sensor data from its plants and a backlog of maintenance decisions waiting on scarce senior engineers. AI agents could read all of it faster than any team. The challenge was to let them help without letting them touch the plant, and to keep the data in the Kingdom.

The situation

An industrial operator in Saudi Arabia ran several processing plants. Maintenance planning depended on a small group of senior engineers who knew the equipment's history, read sensor trends, checked past work orders and decided what to fix, when and with which spares. Their backlog grew every quarter. Data was everywhere: plant historians, a work-order system, inspection reports and spreadsheets of spares, but connecting it for one decision took days.

Why now. Large Gulf industrial companies are moving AI agents into core operations. On 1 November 2026, Aramco and the Public Investment Fund closed a deal giving Aramco 49% of HUMAIN, with Aramco planning to use HUMAIN's AI infrastructure for industrial applications1. A day later, ADNOC announced it would run AI agents on OpenAI's Frontier platform across its operations, hosted on UAE-based infrastructure with human oversight of consequential decisions2. The operator's board wanted the same benefits, with clear limits on what agents could do and where data would live, under Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law34.

What had to be true

  • Agents never touch the plant. No connection to control systems; read-only access to copies of data.
  • One connected view of assets: equipment, relationships, history and spares, current and as at any past date.
  • Every recommendation carries its evidence, so an engineer can check it quickly.
  • Engineers decide. Agents draft; approved changes become normal work orders.
  • Data in the Kingdom, including the personal data in work orders and shift logs.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: giving agents the plant's context, safely

A maintenance recommendation is only as good as its context: what this pump is connected to, how it has behaved, what failed last time and whether the spare is on site. That context was spread across systems that did not agree on names. The team built an asset knowledge graph from an event log rather than from periodic copies. The OpenTelemetry community describes the same pattern for infrastructure: producers emit entity events into a durable, event-sourced log, a live graph is rebuilt from it with full history, and both people and AI assistants query it, the latter through an MCP server5.

Because the graph records when facts were true, an agent can ask what the plant looked like before a past failure, not only what it looks like now. And because agents reach the graph only through read-only MCP tools, with no route back into the plant, the worst a misbehaving agent can do is draft a poor recommendation that an engineer rejects. See entity resolution for knowledge graphs and securing MCP servers.

In industrial settings, the safest agent is one that cannot act. Give it rich context and no levers; let engineers pull the levers.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
One-way export from OTAgents query plant systems directlyNo path from AI back into control systems
Event log feeding a graphNightly copies into a warehouseCurrent state and full history in one model
Read-only MCP toolsAgents with write accessBad drafts get rejected; no bad actions happen
Recommendations, not actionsAgents raise work ordersEngineers stay accountable for the plant
In-Kingdom hostingOverseas model endpointsSimpler PDPL position and board comfort

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: record why engineers rejected or edited recommendations. Those reasons were the best training material for better tools and prompts. Differently: start the asset model with the reliability engineers on day one; naming and relationships were the slowest part to agree. item.title: Tech news, 3 November 2026: Anthropic's compute commitments, ADNOC's AI agents, and exploited Ivanti and Drupal Commerce flaws
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: Anthropic's amended S-1 shows $895B in commitments, ADNOC deploys OpenAI's agent platform, and Ivanti and Drupal Commerce flaws are exploited.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic's amended IPO filing put a number on the cost of frontier AI: hundreds of billions of dollars in commitments, mostly for compute. In Abu Dhabi, the national oil company signed up to run fleets of AI agents across its operations. And two actively exploited flaws, in Ivanti's VPN gateway and in Drupal's e-commerce module, need patching this week.

Today's brief covers stories from 30 October to 2 November that earlier briefs did not include.

1. Anthropic's amended S-1 shows the scale of AI compute commitments

Anthropic filed an amended IPO registration on 2 November adding third-quarter results, with revenue of about $17 billion for the quarter, and disclosed about $895.4 billion of purchase commitments and lease agreements1. Coverage reports nine-month revenue of $33.2 billion and says substantially all of the commitments relate to compute and infrastructure2.

CTO take: the model providers you build on are making very long, very large bets on compute. That is good for capacity, but it also means pricing, contracts and capacity allocation will be shaped by their need to fill those commitments. Keep your stack portable across providers and know your cost per task; see planning around the AI capacity crunch and model routing.

2. ADNOC signs up to run AI agents with OpenAI and G42

ADNOC announced a multi-year agreement with OpenAI and G42 on 2 November to build and run AI agents on OpenAI's Frontier platform across its operations, including forecasting crude supply, demand, prices and margins3. The systems will run on G42's UAE-based infrastructure, with human experts keeping oversight of consequential decisions; financial terms were not disclosed4.

CTO take: agent platforms are moving from pilots into core operations at large industrial firms, with in-country hosting and human sign-off built into the deal. If you sell into Gulf enterprises, expect buyers to ask for exactly that combination. See when agents become the user and the UAE page.

3. CISA adds two more Ivanti Connect Secure flaws to its exploited list

CISA added two Ivanti Connect Secure vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 30 October, with federal patch deadlines in early and mid-November5. The Hacker News reports attackers chaining Connect Secure flaws to gain unauthenticated root access6.

CTO take: VPN gateways remain the front door attackers try first. Patch now, check for signs of compromise rather than assuming the patch is enough, and keep the management interface off the internet. The pattern is covered in hardening a utility's management plane.

4. A highly critical Drupal Commerce flaw is being exploited

Drupal says an access bypass in the Commerce Core module, CVE-2026-118539, is being actively exploited, and asks store owners to update and audit their orders for inconsistencies78. Commerce Core is a contributed module, not Drupal core itself.

CTO take: if you run Drupal Commerce, update to the fixed release named in Drupal's advisory today and review recent orders and payments. For older stores, this is a good moment to inventory which contributed modules handle money and who maintains them.

What I'd do this week

  • Patch Ivanti Connect Secure and Drupal Commerce if you run them, then check for compromise.
  • Review your AI provider contracts for pricing and capacity terms that could change.
  • If you sell into Gulf enterprises, prepare an answer on in-country hosting and human oversight for agents.
